label: Women’s hospital deaths that were maternal
plain_language: Of every 100 women aged 15-49 who died in these hospitals, 5 died from pregnancy or childbirth.
headline: yes

label: Deaths from direct obstetric causes
plain_language: Five in six maternal deaths came from direct causes of pregnancy and birth; the rest from conditions like anaemia and heart disease.

label: Eclampsia
plain_language: Eclampsia - dangerously high blood pressure with seizures in pregnancy - was the single biggest killer, and it hit the youngest women hardest.
headline: yes

label: Obstetric haemorrhage
plain_language: Heavy bleeding around birth was the second leading cause, and its share rose over the decade.

label: Maternal sepsis
plain_language: Infection around pregnancy and birth caused about 1 in 6 deaths, often alongside unsafe abortion.

label: Abortion-related
plain_language: Complications of abortion caused about 1 in 9 deaths; the share eased slightly over the ten years.

label: Ruptured uterus
plain_language: A ruptured womb, usually from obstructed labour, caused about 1 in 14 deaths and was more common in older women.

label: Anaemia (indirect)
plain_language: Severe anaemia was the leading indirect cause, and was closely tied to deaths from bleeding.

label: Cardiovascular (indirect)
plain_language: Heart and blood-vessel problems caused about 1 in 7 deaths, and rose sharply over the decade.

label: Hospital death rate, 2006 to 2015
plain_language: The hospital maternal death rate climbed by more than 40% over the decade, peaking in 2011.
headline: yes

label: Haemorrhage share, first half vs second
plain_language: Bleeding claimed a growing share of deaths, rising from 21% in the first five years to 27% in the second.

label: Teenage-mother deaths, first half vs second
plain_language: Deaths among mothers aged 15-19 fell markedly, from 17.8% of maternal deaths to 11.1%.

label: Deaths among women aged 20-34
plain_language: Two thirds of the women who died were aged 20-34 - the years when most births happen.
